## Part 1: The traditional reading, verse by verse

**Overview.** Ellicott divides the chapter into three parts: the riddle (vv. 3–10), its explanation (vv. 11–21), and a "clear Messianic prophecy" (vv. 22–24). He reads the chapter with chapters 8–19 and points to the history in 2 Kings 24, 2 Chronicles 36 and Jeremiah 37 and 52. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/17.htm
- Precept Austin suggests a date of about 592–591 BC. That would mean Ezekiel foretold Zedekiah's revolt about three years before it happened, though it says we can't be dogmatic about the date. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel-17-commentary
- Matthew Henry's framing: chapter 16 dealt with Judah breaking covenant with God. Chapter 17 deals with the king breaking covenant with the king of Babylon. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_017.cfm

**v. 1**
- Precept Austin: the opening line marks what follows as God's revelation to the exiled prophet, not Ezekiel's own opinion. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel-17-commentary

**v. 2**
- Ellicott: it is a "riddle" because it is obscure and meant to make people guess, and a "parable" because it is a comparison. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/17.htm
- Gill: the Hebrew literally reads "whet a whetting." The form was chosen not to hide the message but to stir attention and fix it in memory. He stresses that the riddle is God's, not the prophet's. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/17.htm
- Guzik (quoting Feinberg and Morgan): chapter 16 dealt with Israel's spiritual and moral sickness, while chapter 17 deals with her political folly. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-17/
- Matthew Henry: ministers should look for "acceptable words" and use familiar images in preaching. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_017.cfm

**v. 3**
- **The eagle.** Ellicott identifies it as Nebuchadnezzar, with eagle imagery also used in Jeremiah 48 and 49. Its broad wings mean conquests far and wide. Its many-coloured feathers mean the many nations and languages in his empire. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/17.htm
- **Lebanon** is Jerusalem, as in Jeremiah 22:23. The reason is all the cedar in the royal palace, which was called "the house of the forest of Lebanon." Ellicott also suggests translating "highest branch" as "topshoot." (same page)
- **Gill's alternatives.** "Lebanon" could mean either the whole land or Jerusalem with its cedar-built temple. He takes the feathers to stand for cities, armies and wealth. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/17.htm
- **NET notes.** Hebrew has two words for "wings," and it is unclear whether they mean exactly the same thing. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=eze%2017:2-10

**v. 4**
- **The top shoot** is Jehoiachin, carried off to Babylon (Ellicott, Matthew Henry). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/17.htm ; https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_017.cfm
- **"Land of traffic."** Ellicott notes the Hebrew literally says "land of Canaan," a word that can mean "merchant." Babylon gets the same label in 16:29 because of its trade. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/17.htm
- Keil and Delitzsch (apparently) say the same: Babylon's trading spirit made it "a Canaan." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/17-3.htm
- Matthew Henry adds a light touch: a king of David's line would feel disgraced living among tradesmen, "but he must make the best of it." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_017.cfm

**v. 5**
- Ellicott: instead of putting a foreign governor over the land, Nebuchadnezzar appointed a native prince, Zedekiah, Jehoiachin's uncle. He was planted not as a tall cedar but as a willow that could thrive in its own modest way. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/17.htm
- NET: "seedling" suits the plant picture, but in the explanation "seed" means offspring, i.e. Zedekiah. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=eze%2017:2-10
- Matthew Henry: Nebuchadnezzar set the plant "with circumspection," letting it grow but not too big. He also notes the name change from Mattaniah to Zedekiah ("justice of the Lord"). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_017.cfm

**v. 6**
- **Ellicott.** Had Zedekiah stayed loyal to his oath, and to God above that, Judah could have prospered as a dependent kingdom. He suggests translating "*that* its branches might turn toward him." Nebuchadnezzar wanted a thriving but dependent buffer state against Egypt. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/17.htm
- **Gill.** Judah was no longer a cedar but a vine: it might flourish, but it runs along the ground and leans on something else. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/17.htm
- **Clarke** describes Judah's dependence the same way. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/ezekiel/17.htm
- **Precept Austin.** There was real potential for life even in this reduced state, but Judah's welfare depended on humble submission to the authority God had appointed. One source it quotes adds that Jerusalem would no longer be a cedar because of past evil, especially under Manasseh. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel-17-commentary

**v. 7**
- **The second eagle** is Pharaoh. He is powerful, but Ellicott notes he lacks the many colours, because he did not rule as many peoples. Persuading Zedekiah away from this Egyptian alliance was a main task of Jeremiah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/17.htm
- NET identifies him as Pharaoh Hophra. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=eze%2017:2-10
- Guzik (quoting Block) notes how passive this eagle is: he does nothing, he is just "there." Guzik also stresses that the vine sought from Egypt what it already had. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-17/
- Keil and Delitzsch (apparently): the Hebrew verb means to yearn or pine for something. The vine had no need to reach out, since it could thrive where it was planted. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/17-1.htm
- Matthew Henry: the vine bent her roots toward Egypt secretly at first, then openly. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_017.cfm

**v. 8**
- Guzik: the vine's tragic flaw was not lack of resources but its foolish choice to turn away from its first patron. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-17/
- Bible.org (Utley) offers two readings. Either the verse shows how Zedekiah imagined Egypt would help him, or it repeats v. 5 to show he had no need to rebel. https://bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-17
- Precept Austin: had Zedekiah obeyed, he would have thrived and his children would have lived. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel-17-commentary

**v. 9**
- **"He"** who pulls up the roots is Nebuchadnezzar (Gill, Clarke). The leaves withering "in spring" means ruin in the middle of prosperity. Needing no "great power" shows how easily Babylon would do it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/17.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/ezekiel/17.htm
- **Ellicott reads the last clause differently.** It means that not even a great army could raise the vine up again. In other words, Pharaoh's strength could not restore what God had blighted (compare v. 17). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/17.htm
- NET notes the uncertain rare words in this verse. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=eze%2017:2-10
- Matthew Henry: God "needs not great power and many people" to accomplish his purposes. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_017.cfm
- Precept Austin quotes Woodhead's claim that v. 9 contains every letter of the Hebrew alphabet. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel-17-commentary

**v. 10**
- Precept Austin (Woodhead): the east wind is Babylon, which lay to the northeast. It is hot and dries things out. The irony is that the vine dies in the very bed where it was given every chance. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel-17-commentary
- Guzik (quoting Block): by turning its branches up and its roots outward, the vine made itself more exposed to the wind. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-17/
- Keil and Delitzsch (apparently): the east wind is especially dangerous to plants because it is so dry (compare Genesis 41:6). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/17-1.htm

**v. 11**
- Ellicott thinks some time probably passed between the riddle and its explanation, so the people would be keener to hear the meaning. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/17.htm

**v. 12**
- Gill: Israel is called "rebellious" against God and now also against Babylon. Anyone who knew current events could have solved the riddle. He also notes that some ancient versions put these verses in the future tense, while the history requires the past. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/17.htm
- Guzik sets out the key: eagle = Babylon, Lebanon = Jerusalem, top shoot = Jehoiachin and the princes, seed/vine = Zedekiah. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-17/

**v. 13**
- Gill: "the mighty" (literally "the rams" of the land) were taken both to weaken the nation and as hostages to guarantee the treaty. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/17.htm
- Guzik says those taken included Daniel and his companions. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-17/
- Bible.org: the oath was taken in the LORD's name (2 Chronicles 36:13). https://bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-17

**v. 14**
- Gill: the treaty was actually for Judah's good. Without it, Judah would have become just a Babylonian province. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/17.htm
- Matthew Henry: God brought judgment step by step, making the kingdom "base" before ending it, to give space to repent. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_017.cfm
- Precept Austin: submission was a God-given way to survive, so breaking the treaty was resisting God himself. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel-17-commentary

**v. 15**
- Ellicott: breaking an oath was especially hateful to God. He compares the Gibeonite oath, which God still enforced centuries later even though it was obtained by fraud (2 Samuel 21). Zedekiah had also been warned through Jeremiah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/17.htm
- Matthew Henry: sin had brought God's people so low that their king had to send to Egypt for "much people." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_017.cfm

**v. 16**
- Ellicott: Zedekiah's death in Babylon fits the crime, since he dies in the land of the king he betrayed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/17.htm
- Gill: "As I live" is God swearing by his own life (citing Kimchi). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/17.htm
- Bible.org cross-references Jeremiah 52:11. https://bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-17

**v. 17**
- Ellicott: the siege mounds belong to the besieging army, so the line should read "when they cast up mounts." The Pharaoh was Hophra (Jeremiah 44:30). Egypt's army did briefly lift the siege (Jeremiah 37), but it achieved nothing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/17.htm
- Matthew Henry: God "commonly weakens and withers that arm of flesh which we trust in." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/ezekiel/17.htm

**v. 18**
- Precept Austin: "gave his hand" was a formal pledge (NET note: compare 2 Kings 10:15). It shows a heart that says one thing and does another. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel-17-commentary
- Matthew Henry argues from lesser to greater: if breaking a human oath is punished like this, breaking covenant with God deserves far worse (Hebrews 10). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_017.cfm
- Guzik (quoting Feinberg): once he had given his hand, that word should have been all the bond needed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-17/

**v. 19**
- Ellicott: the oath and covenant are called "My" (God's) because they were sworn in the LORD's name. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/17.htm
- Guzik (quoting Alexander): God would bring on Zedekiah the curses he had called down on himself in his oath. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-17/
- Matthew Henry: perjury is a "heinous sin," and being a king was no excuse. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/ezekiel/17.htm

**v. 20**
- Guzik: breaking faith with Nebuchadnezzar was treason against God. As Jeremiah urged, Zedekiah should have surrendered. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-17/
- Bible.org links the net to 12:13 and to the history in 2 Kings. https://bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-17
- Matthew Henry: by rebelling, Zedekiah falls deeper into Babylon's hands, because God now takes Babylon's side. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_017.cfm

**v. 21**
- Guzik: there would be no recovery, and Judea would be fully conquered. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-17/
- Pulpit Commentary: this verse repeats 12:14–15. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/17.htm
- Precept Austin: a local revolt ends in the nation unravelling. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel-17-commentary

**v. 22**
- **Ellicott.** Until now God worked through human agents. Here he steps in directly and takes a shoot of David's royal "cedar." He says "nearly all interpreters, Jewish and Christian" take this to be the Messiah, and "tender" points to his lowly human origins. He links it to the "Branch" passages (Isaiah 11:1; 4:2; Jeremiah 23:5). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/17-22.htm
- **Gill.** He reads each detail: the high cedar = the Jewish nation, the highest branch = Judah, the young twigs = David's family, the tender one = the Messiah. He says the Jewish commentator Jarchi (Rashi) and the Targum agree, while Kimchi thought of Zerubbabel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/17-22.htm
- **Calvin.** The "tender" twig shows "the contemptible beginning of the reign of Christ." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/17-22.html
- **Matthew Henry.** Christ was the highest branch, furthest from the root but nearest to heaven. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/ezekiel/17.htm
- **Guzik.** The tender twig is the Messiah, Ezekiel's version of Isaiah 11:1. God says emphatically, "*I myself* will plant it." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-17/

**v. 23**
- **Ellicott.** The Christian era is rooted in the Jewish one ("the law shall go forth from Zion"). The mountain stands for the centre of the kingdom and shouldn't be tied too literally to the hill of Zion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/17-23.htm
- **Gill.** He takes it literally of Jerusalem, where the Messiah preached and the first church was planted. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/17-23.htm
- **The birds.** Geneva Bible notes: Jews and Gentiles gathered in. Poole (quoted by Guzik): all nations, no longer only the Jews. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/17-23.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-17/
- **Links to Jesus' parable.** One excerpt (apparently JFB) calls this tree the Gospel "mustard tree" of Matthew 13:32 and contrasts it with the proud trees of Assyria and Babylon (Ezekiel 31; Daniel 4). Barnes also cross-references Matthew 13:32. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/17-23.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/ezekiel-17.html
- **Keil and Delitzsch (apparently).** "Birds of every wing" echoes the birds in Noah's ark (Genesis 7:14) and stands for people of every nation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/17-23.htm

**v. 24**
- **Keil and Delitzsch (apparently).** This is a general truth, like Hannah's song in 1 Samuel 2. It hints at David's house and Jehoiachin but isn't limited to them. The "trees of the field" are other kings and kingdoms. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/17-23.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/17-24.htm
- **Spurgeon** preached on this verse: since the Fall, God has purposed to bring down everything set up against him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/ezekiel-17.html
- **Utley.** "I have spoken, and I will do it" means people can rely on both God's judgments and his promises. https://bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-17
- **Morgan (via Precept Austin).** The lasting point is God's sovereignty, and restoration comes by his power, not by rebellious politics. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel-17-commentary

---

## Part 2: Where the traditions differ (vv. 22–24)

Every source I read takes vv. 22–24 as messianic. They differ on how the prophecy is fulfilled, not on what it is about.

- **Zerubbabel first, or Christ alone?**
  - The Benson Commentary (a Methodist commentator, from an unlabelled Bible Hub excerpt) says it was partly fulfilled when Zerubbabel returned from exile, but in its "full sense" it fits only Christ. It calls Mount Zion "a type of the gospel church." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/17-22.htm
  - Matthew Henry gives a first application to the Jewish state after Zerubbabel's time. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/ezekiel/17.htm
  - Gill (Baptist) mentions Kimchi's Zerubbabel view but holds to the Messiah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/17-22.htm
  - Ellicott says the passage "can only be" the Messiah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/17-22.htm
- **Fulfilled in the church, or still future?**
  - In the Reformed line, the Geneva notes apply the promise to "the Church," pictured as a small remnant. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/17-22.htm
  - Lange's commentary says the church will not vanish into worldly kingdoms. Instead, those kingdoms will become God's. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lange/ezekiel/17.htm
  - The Pulpit Commentary says the prophecy describes an ideal "never historically realized." It found partial fulfilment in Zerubbabel and the rebuilt temple, but it merges into a still-unfulfilled vision of the Messiah's kingdom and Israel's restoration. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/17.htm
  - Precept Austin says God will keep the Davidic line and his promise of a righteous King. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel-17-commentary
- **What the "trees of the field" are (v. 24).**
  - Benson: all nations, with the "low tree" being the church that God lifts up. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/17-24.htm
  - Keil and Delitzsch (apparently): other royal houses and kingdoms. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/17-24.htm

## Part 3: Other views

- **Modern scholarship.**
  - Guzik quotes the Catholic scholars Vawter and Hoppe: Ezekiel believed "in his fashion" in a restored Davidic dynasty ruling a renewed Israel. This presents the passage as the prophet's hope for Israel rather than a direct prediction of Christ. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-17/
  - The NET notes deal with words rather than theology: the second eagle is Hophra, and the wing terms and some rare words are uncertain. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=eze%2017:2-10
- **Catholic, Orthodox, and prosperity or hyper-grace teaching:** I found nothing on these, so they are left out.
